You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Nvidia NDR Feedback: 95% Growth Still Lacks New Buyers, How Can the 5% Free Cash Flow Yield Open Up Value Funds?

TEXT:
Dozens of investor communications following Nvidia’s roadshow sent a clear signal: the market remains optimistic about near-term revenues, and the points of divergence have shifted toward who will keep buying, the quality of customer diversification, and the extent to which new cloud credit support will bring incremental returns and risks. Whether the 95% growth rate and over 5% free cash flow yield can attract value-driven capital will determine if the valuation discount can narrow.
1. Feedback After the Roadshow Exposes Contradictions at the Equity Level
There is now a high degree of consensus on near-term fundamentals, but the stock’s performance has not kept pace. Morgan Stanley’s July 13 semiconductor weekly review revisited Nvidia’s NDR from the previous week, summarizing dozens of post-non-deal roadshow investor exchanges. Professional investors broadly agree on Nvidia’s strong near-term earnings prospects; the most common question now is: with growth remaining strong, how can the stock outperform its semiconductor peers once again?
The report does not identify a definite near-term catalyst. Rather, it frames the issue as one related to portfolio structure. Nvidia’s massive market cap and high index weighting mean many growth funds have reached sizable positions, in some cases close to their internal limits for single stocks. Recently, most mid-to-large-cap semiconductor companies have attracted incremental capital, but Nvidia lacks new marginal buyers. Even as fundamentals improve, the valuation discount may persist for a while.
This forms a clear division of topics compared to the previous NDR. The last session focused on the sources of growth: increasing market share in artificial intelligence (AI) labs, continued expansion by hyperscale cloud players, and secondary demand from AI cloud, industrial, enterprise, and sovereign projects; additionally, Vera CPU, networking, and Rubin systems continue to boost Nvidia’s value per data center. This week’s report addresses whether investors are willing to further increase their positions now that these themes are accepted by the capital markets.
Nvidia Roadshow Deep Dive: GB300 Token Per Watt, ACIE’s Half of Revenue, and $1-Trillion Blackwell and Rubin Visibility
2. 95% Growth Is Strong, But Hard To Create Surprises On Its Own
The market hardly questions Nvidia’s continued strong revenue momentum. Morgan Stanley cites a quarterly growth rate of 95%, which comes before the next major product cycle. Management continues to emphasize that the growth pace will accelerate. Although there’s debate around longer-term growth, market share, and margins, there’s little dissent regarding robust operations in the coming quarters.
Such consensus favors earnings but complicates stock price catalysts. Most investors already believe in Blackwell’s next ramp and in Rubin taking up the baton. Another earnings beat will only yield further upside if it vastly exceeds already elevated market expectations. Simply demonstrating strong demand might validate earnings projections—but it’s hard to explain why new capital must be deployed right now.
Nvidia needs to translate its growth story into cash returns. The roadshow is proactively courting value, yield-focused accounts, and family offices, while still serving legacy growth capital. This move signals management has accepted a new reality: the world’s largest company by market cap cannot rely solely on growth funds to expand its holder base; valuation rerating requires new categories of capital.
3. Over 5% Free Cash Flow Yield Is the Entry Point for New Buyers
Cash flow is becoming Nvidia’s second valuation language. Morgan Stanley expects, on a forward-12-month basis, Nvidia’s free cash flow yield to exceed 5%, with more than 50% of this potentially returned to shareholders. Together, this implies over 2.5% of market cap in potential annual cash returns, possibly via buybacks and dividends—the exact yield will depend on execution price and timing.
Growth funds prioritize revenue growth, the Rubin roadmap, and per-token cost. Value and yield funds care more about whether free cash flow remains steady during product transitions, if buybacks can continuously lift per-share value, and whether cash returns can provide a valuation floor during any market pullbacks. Nvidia is working to meet both standards simultaneously.
The previous full roadshow materials already suggested plans to return over 50% of free cash flow. This round of investor feedback indicates that the number is starting to reshape the shareholder structure; capital allocation policies are morphing into the new valuation anchor. Morgan Stanley maintains Nvidia as its top semiconductor pick, setting a reference price of $211 and a base target price of $288 on July 13; bear and bull case targets are $160 and $330, respectively. The $288 target equates to about 37% upside. Whether the valuation gap narrows will depend on whether new money really deploys.
[...]
Cash returns can’t overshadow supply chain commitments. Nvidia needs to pre-secure wafer, advanced packaging, memory, networking, and full system capacity. Should demand be misjudged, inventory, prepayments, and purchase obligations would weigh on cash conversion first. Value investors will only step in if free cash flow stays robust, even through Rubin transitions, export constraints, or client financing volatility.
[...]
Diversification cuts both ways. Nvidia faces less competition from custom chips and more whole-system and software sales opportunities, while client credit, financing costs, deployment speeds, and local regulation differences grow. A broader revenue base does not guarantee higher revenue quality.
[...]
The new cloud cooperation model is the focal point of the next debate. Nvidia plans to offer broader credit support to new cloud customers in exchange for a share of cloud services revenue. After selling hardware, the company could also receive further revenue from GPU cloud operations. Morgan Stanley believes that when compute remains scarce, such revenue sharing could yield recurring income at nearly 100% gross margin.
[...]
The upside thesis is straightforward. Nvidia uses its credit capacity to help customers expand financing and procurement, boosting hardware sales; once the new cloud platform goes live, it gets revenue sharing. The business extends from a one-off system supplier to holding economic interests in GPU cloud networks. As long as client utilization is high, rental prices are stable, and payments flow smoothly, the model boosts both revenue scale and profit margins.
[...]
But the risks must be accounted for separately. Credit support may take the form of guarantees, buyback commitments, minimum income arrangements, or other contingencies—the costs may not be immediately reflected in the P&L. If a new cloud customer faces financing trouble, low utilization, or falling rental prices, hardware revenue may already have been booked while credit losses surface later. The market must distinguish between “end demand from clients” and “clients who pre-purchase equipment using Nvidia’s credit support.”
[...]
Nvidia has confirmed memory shortages may persist for years, and will proactively seek ways to reduce per-system memory consumption. This has stirred concerns among storage investors: if Nvidia lowers per-cabinet memory usage through architecture optimization, will DRAM prices and shipment elasticity be suppressed?
[...]
Rubin Will Devour Mobile Memory in 2027: Why Nvidia Is Taking Phone DRAM — How Vera Rubin Will Rewrite DRAM Output Rankings
[...]
Remaining steadily over 5% will decide if value capital can include Nvidia within its cash return framework.
